paragraphs: “I was living a wild life then. Father said just now that I spent several thousand roubles seducing young girls. That’s a swinish invention, and nothing of the sort happened. And if it did, I didn’t need money for _that_. For me money is an accessory, the overflow of my heart, the scenery. Today she would be my lady; tomorrow a girl off the streets would take her place. I entertained them both. I threw money away by the handful on music, carousing and gypsies. Sometimes I gave it to the ladies too, because they take it greedily, I have to admit, and they’re pleased and grateful for it. Ladies used to like me. Not all of them, but it happened, it happened. But I always liked side-paths, the little dark back-alleys behind the main road. That’s where you find adventures and surprises, and precious metal in the dirt. I’m speaking figuratively, brother. In the town I was living in there were no such back-alleys in the literal sense, but morally there were. If you were like me, you’d know what that means. I loved vice, I loved the shame of vice. I loved cruelty. Am I not a bug, a noxious insect? A Karamazov, in short! Once a whole crowd of us went on a picnic, in seven sledges. It was dark, it was winter, and I started squeezing a girl’s hand and made her kiss me. She was an official’s daughter, a sweet, gentle, submissive creature. She let me, she let me do a great deal in the dark. She thought, poor thing, that I would come the next day to propose to her (I was considered a good match, too). But I didn’t say a word to her for five months. I would see her in a corner at dances (we were always having dances), her eyes following me. I saw how they glowed with fire, a fire of gentle indignation. This game only tickled the insect lust I nursed in my soul. Five months later she married an official and left the town, still angry, and still, maybe, in love with me. Now they live happily. Mind you, I told no one. I didn’t boast of it. Though I’m full of low desires and love what’s low, I’m not dishonorable. You’re blushing; your eyes flashed. That’s enough of this filth with you. And all this was nothing much—wayside blossoms _à la_ Paul de Kock—though the cruel insect had already grown strong in my soul. I’ve got a perfect album of memories, brother. God bless them, the darlings. I tried to end things without a quarrel. And I never gave them away. I never bragged about a single one of them. But that’s enough. You can’t think I brought you here just to talk about such nonsense. No, I’m going to tell you something more curious, and don’t be surprised that I’m glad to tell you, instead of being ashamed.”
“You say that because I blushed,” Alyosha said suddenly. “I wasn’t blushing at what you were saying or at what you’ve done. I blushed because I’m the same as you are.”
“You? Come on, that’s going a little too far!”

“No, it’s not too far,” said Alyosha warmly (obviously the idea was not a new one to him). “The ladder is the same. I’m on the bottom step and you’re above, somewhere around the thirteenth. That’s how I see it. But it’s all the same. Exactly the same in kind. Anyone on the bottom step is bound to go up to the top one.”
“Then one shouldn’t step on at all.”
“Anyone who can help it had better not.”

“Hush, Alyosha, hush, darling! I could kiss your hand, you touch me so. That rogue Grushenka has an eye for men. She told me once that she’d devour you one day. There, there, I won’t! Let’s leave this field of corruption, fouled by flies, and move on to my tragedy, also fouled by flies, that is, by every sort of vileness. The old man told lies about my seducing innocence, but there really was something of the sort in my tragedy, though it happened only once, and then it didn’t come off. The old man who reproaches me with what never happened doesn’t even know about this; I never told anyone. You’re the first, except Ivan, of course—Ivan knows everything. He knew about it long before you. But Ivan’s a tomb.”

“I was a lieutenant in a line regiment, but I was still under supervision, like a kind of convict. Yet I was received awfully well in the little town. I spent money right and left. They thought I was rich; I thought so myself. But I must have pleased them in other ways as well. They shook their heads over me, but they liked me. My colonel, who was an old man, took a sudden dislike to me. He was always down on me, but I had powerful friends, and besides, the whole town was on my side, so he couldn’t do me much harm. I was partly to blame myself, because I refused to treat him with proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old fellow, who was really a very good sort, kind-hearted and hospitable, had had two wives, both dead. His first wife, who came from a humble family, left a daughter as unpretentious as herself. She was a young woman of twenty-four when I was there, and lived with her father and an aunt, her mother’s sister. The aunt was simple and unlettered; the niece was simple but lively. I like to say nice things about people. I never knew a woman with a more charming character than Agafya—imagine, her name was Agafya Ivanovna! And she wasn’t bad-looking either, in the Russian style: tall, stout, full-figured, with beautiful eyes, though a rather coarse face. She hadn’t married, although she’d had two suitors. She turned them down, but stayed as cheerful as ever. I was close to her, not in ‘that’ way, it was pure friendship. I’ve often been friends with women quite innocently. I used to talk to her with shocking frankness, and she only laughed. Many women like such freedom, and she was a girl too, which made it very amusing. Another thing: you could never think of her as a young lady. She and her aunt lived in her father’s house with a sort of voluntary humility, not putting themselves on an equal footing with other people. She was a general favorite and useful to everyone, because she was a clever dressmaker. She had a talent for it. She gave her services freely, without asking for payment, but if anyone offered her payment, she didn’t refuse. The colonel, of course, was a very different matter. He was one of the chief personages in the district. He kept open house, entertained the whole town, gave suppers and dances. At the time I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole town was talking about the expected return of the colonel’s second daughter, a great beauty, who had just left a fashionable school in the capital. This second daughter is Katerina Ivanovna, the child of the second wife, who came from the family of a distinguished general. Although, as I learned on good authority, she too brought the colonel no money. She had connections, and that was all. There may have been expectations, but they had come to nothing.

“Yet when the young lady came home from boarding-school for a visit, the whole town came to life. Our most distinguished ladies—two ‘Excellencies’ and a colonel’s wife—and everyone else following their lead, took her up at once and gave entertainments in her honor. She was the belle of the balls and picnics, and they got up _tableaux vivants_ to raise money for distressed governesses. I took no notice. I went on as wildly as before, and one of my exploits at the time set the whole town talking. One evening at the battery commander’s I saw her eyes sizing me up, but I didn’t go over to her, as though I disdained her acquaintance. I did go up and speak to her at an evening party not long after. She hardly looked at me and pressed her lips together scornfully. ‘Wait a bit. I’ll have my revenge,’ I thought. I behaved like an awful fool on many occasions at that time, and I knew it myself. What made it worse was that I felt ‘Katenka’ was not an innocent boarding-school miss, but a person of character, proud and truly high-principled. Above all, she had education and intellect, and I had neither. You think I meant to propose to her? No, I simply wanted revenge, because I was such a hero and she didn’t seem to feel it.

“Meanwhile I spent my time in drink and riot, until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Just then father sent me six thousand roubles, in return for my sending him a deed giving up all claims on him—settling our accounts, so to speak, and saying I wouldn’t expect anything more. I didn’t understand a word of it at the time. Until I came here, Alyosha, until the last few days, in fact, and maybe even now, I haven’t been able to make head or tail of my money affairs with father. But never mind that, we’ll talk about it later.

“Just as I received the money, I got a letter from a friend telling me something that interested me immensely. The authorities, I learned, were dissatisfied with our lieutenant-colonel. He was suspected of irregularities; in fact, his enemies were preparing a surprise for him. Then the commander of the division arrived and kicked up the devil of a row. Shortly afterwards the colonel was ordered to retire. I won’t tell you how it all came about. He certainly had enemies. Suddenly the town turned noticeably cool toward him and his whole family. His friends all turned their backs on him. Then I took my first step. I met Agafya Ivanovna, with whom I’d always kept up a friendship, and said, ‘Do you know there’s a shortage of 4,500 roubles of government money in your father’s accounts?’
